title: Freedom's Boundaries, At Home and Abroad
summary: The 1890s opened with dramatic clashes between capital and labor and a massive farmers' revolt. The 1892 Homestead Strike, crushed by Pinkerton agents and state militia, showed that even strong unions could not stand up to giant corporations. Meanwhile, farmers in the South and West, squeezed by falling crop prices, debt, and railroad freight charges, built the Farmers' Alliance and then the People's (Populist) Party. Its 1892 Omaha platform demanded a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, government control of currency, and public ownership of railroads. The depression that began in 1893 brought Coxey's Army and the Pullman Strike, both put down by federal power. In 1896, Democrat William Jennings Bryan ran on free silver but lost to Republican William McKinley, whose lavishly funded campaign forged a Republican majority that lasted until 1932.

In the South, Populism's defeat cleared the way for a hardened racial order. Between 1890 and 1906 every southern state stripped Black men of the vote through poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses, while the Supreme Court blessed segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) under the fiction of 'separate but equal.' Lynching enforced the system through terror, prompting Ida B. Wells's crusade against mob violence. Booker T. Washington's 1895 Atlanta address urged Black southerners to accept segregation and pursue economic self-help. Nationally, freedom's boundaries narrowed as well: Chinese immigrants faced exclusion, nativists organized against southern and eastern Europeans, the AFL limited itself to skilled white workers, and suffragists increasingly appealed to racial and ethnic hierarchy.

Abroad, the United States became an imperial power. After American planters toppled Hawaii's queen in 1893, the islands were annexed in 1898 amid the Spanish-American War, sparked by Cuba's independence struggle and the sinking of the U.S.S. Maine. The quick victory brought Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines under American rule, while the Platt Amendment made Cuba a protectorate. Suppressing Filipino independence required a far bloodier war (1899–1903), and the Insular Cases ruled that the Constitution did not fully follow the flag, leaving Americans to debate whether the republic had become an empire.
big_ideas: The Populist movement was the era's largest political insurgency, demanding that the federal government curb corporate power and restore economic opportunity for small producers.
The election of 1896 pitted Bryan's free-silver coalition of the South and West against McKinley's industrial Northeast and Midwest, producing a durable Republican majority.
During the 1890s southern states legally disenfranchised Black voters and, with the Supreme Court's approval in Plessy v. Ferguson, built a comprehensive Jim Crow system enforced by lynching.
Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise urged accommodation to segregation and economic self-help, a strategy later challenged by W. E. B. Du Bois's demand for full civil and political rights.

The boundaries of American freedom contracted for many groups at once: Chinese exclusion, nativism toward new European immigrants, a narrower AFL, and a suffrage movement that embraced racial arguments.
The Spanish-American War of 1898 made the United States an overseas empire ruling Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and the Philippine War revealed the violence behind 'benevolent' imperialism.
The Insular Cases and the Platt Amendment showed that the new colonial subjects would be governed without the constitutional rights or consent Americans claimed as fundamental.

key_terms.def: Political party formed in 1892 out of the Farmers' Alliance that spoke for indebted farmers and some workers, calling for currency reform, a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, and public ownership of railroads.

Violent confrontation at Andrew Carnegie's Pennsylvania steelworks in which strikers battled Pinkerton guards before the state militia reopened the plant, destroying the union and demonstrating corporate dominance over labor.
March of unemployed men to Washington led by Jacob Coxey demanding federal job creation and currency expansion during the 1893 depression; it was dispersed by soldiers.
Nationwide railroad boycott led by Eugene V. Debs's American Railway Union that was broken by a federal court injunction and troops; the Supreme Court upheld Debs's jailing in In re Debs.
Nebraska Democrat whose 'Cross of Gold' speech won him the 1896 nomination on a free-silver platform; he lost to McKinley but fused Democratic and Populist reform energies.
Supreme Court ruling that state-mandated racial segregation was constitutional if facilities were 'separate but equal'; Justice Harlan dissented that the Constitution is color-blind.

Elimination of Black (and many poor white) voters in the South between 1890 and 1906 through poll taxes, literacy tests, understanding clauses, and grandfather clauses that evaded the Fifteenth Amendment on paper.

Provision exempting men whose ancestors could vote before the Civil War from new suffrage requirements, protecting illiterate whites while excluding Black voters; struck down by the Supreme Court in 1915.
Mob murder, usually of Black men in the South, used to terrorize African Americans and enforce white supremacy; journalist Ida B. Wells led the national campaign against it.
Migration of roughly 40,000–60,000 Black southerners to Kansas in 1879–1880 seeking land, schooling, and safety from violence in the post-Reconstruction South.
Booker T. Washington's speech urging Black Americans to accept segregation for the time being and concentrate on vocational training and economic advancement, a stance critics like Du Bois rejected.
First federal law to bar an immigrant group on racial grounds, halting Chinese immigration; it was renewed, made permanent in 1902, and paired with registration and deportation policies.
Craft-union federation led by Samuel Gompers that pursued 'business unionism'—better wages and hours for skilled, mostly white, native-born male workers—rather than broad social reform.
American battleship that exploded in Havana harbor in February 1898, killing about 270; though likely accidental, the sinking, amplified by the yellow press, pushed the nation toward war with Spain.
Provision forced into Cuba's constitution authorizing U.S. military intervention on the island and granting naval bases, including Guantánamo Bay, making Cuba an American protectorate.
Supreme Court decisions holding that constitutional rights did not fully extend to Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and other new territories, allowing rule over colonial subjects without their consent.

timeline.event: Kansas Exodus begins as tens of thousands of Black southerners migrate west seeking freedom and opportunity
Chinese Exclusion Act bars Chinese immigration, the first race-based federal immigration ban
Homestead Strike is crushed; the People's Party adopts its Omaha platform and runs James Weaver for president
American planters overthrow Queen Liliuokalani in Hawaii; a severe economic depression begins
Coxey's Army marches on Washington and the Pullman Strike is broken by federal troops and injunctions
Booker T. Washington delivers his Atlanta Compromise address
Plessy v. Ferguson upholds 'separate but equal'; McKinley defeats Bryan in a realigning election
Spanish-American War: victories at Manila Bay and Santiago bring Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines; Hawaii is annexed
Philippine War begins against Emilio Aguinaldo's independence movement; John Hay announces the Open Door Policy
Gold Standard Act passes and McKinley defeats Bryan again in an election framed as 'republic or empire'
Platt Amendment binds Cuba to U.S. oversight; the Insular Cases begin limiting constitutional rights in the territories

themes: Politics and power: Populism, the 1896 realignment, and southern disenfranchisement show fierce contests over who controls government and who may vote.
Work, exchange, and technology: Homestead and Pullman revealed the imbalance between industrial corporations and labor, while farmers battled railroads, creditors, and the gold standard.
American and national identity: Jim Crow, Chinese exclusion, and nativism narrowed who counted as a full citizen, even as reformers contested those limits.
America in the world: The Spanish-American War, the Philippine War, and the Open Door marked the U.S. debut as an overseas imperial and commercial power.
Migration and settlement: The Kansas Exodus and the surge of 'new immigrants' from southern and eastern Europe reshaped debates over freedom and belonging.
